prompt: caio holds `AdministratorAccess`, yet his `assume-role` on `deployer` is refused. Why?
hint: Two policies have to agree.

choices.text: `AdministratorAccess` leaves out the `sts` actions
choices.why: It allows `*` on `*`, which includes `sts:AssumeRole`. His side agreed.

choices.text: The role's trust policy names bia, and only bia, not him
choices.why: Right. The trust policy is the role's half of the agreement, and no permission of the caller's replaces it.

choices.text: A role gives one session at a time, and bia held it
choices.why: Any number of sessions of one role can exist at once; caio was refused before bia asked.

choices.text: caio has to wait for his key to be accepted by STS
choices.why: The key was accepted: the error names `user/caio`, which only a verified signature reveals.

prompt: bia assumes `deployer`. Whose permissions does the session have?
hint: What did the session's `iam list-users` answer?

choices.text: bia's own, plus the role's
choices.why: Nothing of bia's comes along. Roles do not add to a caller.

choices.text: The role's, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. bia's policy let her ask for the session; inside it, only the role's policies count.

choices.text: bia's own, since she is the one who signed the call
choices.why: She signed the `AssumeRole` call. The session's calls are signed with the session's key.

choices.text: Only what bia's policy and the role's policy both allow
choices.why: That intersection is how a boundary or a session policy works, not the caller's own policy.

prompt: A trust policy names `"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root"`. In AWS, who can assume the role?
hint: The account decides, through something.

choices.text: Only the root user of that account
choices.why: `:root` here means the account itself, not its root user.

choices.text: Whoever in that account its own policies allow
choices.why: Right. The trust lets the account in; the account's identity policies choose which of its principals.

choices.text: Every principal of every account in the organisation
choices.why: The ARN names one account, and the organisation plays no part in a trust policy unless a condition names it.

choices.text: Nobody, until a user of that account is named as well
choices.why: Naming the account is enough on the role's side; moto refused it, AWS does not.

prompt: In moto, admin was refused a role whose trust policy names admin's own account, `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root`. What does that show?
hint: How does moto compare a caller with a principal?

choices.text: That AWS refuses it too, since admin is not the root user
choices.why: AWS reads `:root` as the account, and admin's `AdministratorAccess` allows the call: AWS gives the session.

choices.text: That moto matches ARNs as plain strings
choices.why: Right. `user/admin` and `root` are different strings; the same comparison breaks role chaining in the next section.

choices.text: That a trust policy may not name the account it belongs to
choices.why: It may, and it is common; the refusal was moto's.

choices.text: That moto's count of free requests had run out for admin
choices.why: The count is spent once, for everybody, and admin's requests have been judged since.

prompt: Put in order what happens when bia assumes `deployer`.
hint: Her side is checked before the role's.
items: bia signs an `AssumeRole` call with her own key
AWS checks that bia's policy allows `sts:AssumeRole` on the role
AWS checks that the role's trust policy names bia
STS returns a key, a secret, a token and an expiry
bia signs her next calls with the session's key
trap: Signing the later calls with her own key is the usual slip: they would act as bia, not as `deployer`.

prompt: Match each question to the policy that answers it.
hint: Three policies, three questions.

pairs.left: may bia ask for the role?

prompt: How many hours is the longest `MaxSessionDuration` a role can be given?
hint: The default is one.

prompt: `deployer` has `MaxSessionDuration` 3600, and bia asks for `--duration-seconds 7200`. What does AWS do, and what did moto do?
hint: Who raises the maximum?

choices.text: Both grant one hour, the most the role allows
choices.why: Neither trims the request. AWS refuses it whole, and moto granted all of it.

choices.text: Both grant two hours, since the caller chooses
choices.why: The caller chooses within the role's maximum; above it, AWS refuses.

choices.text: AWS refuses the request; moto granted two hours
choices.why: Right. The maximum is raised on the role, with `update-role`, not by asking for more. AWS's refusal was not run here.

choices.text: The command line refuses it before sending, in both
choices.why: The command line checks only the floor of 900 seconds, not the role's maximum, which it cannot know.

prompt: Both `deployer` and `auditor` allow twelve-hour sessions. A `deployer` session assumes `auditor` and asks for four hours. What does AWS answer?
hint: This is role chaining.

choices.text: Four hours, since both roles allow twelve
choices.why: Each role's maximum applies to a first session. A chained one has a limit of its own.

choices.text: A refusal: chaining caps it at one hour
choices.why: Right, according to AWS's documentation. That limit was not measured here: moto granted a chained session two hours.

choices.text: Whatever is left of the first session's time
choices.why: The second session's length is not taken from the first's remainder.

choices.text: Twelve hours, the larger of the two maximums
choices.why: Nothing chooses the larger maximum; the request asked for four and is refused for exceeding one.

prompt: Why is a source identity stronger evidence of who did something than a session name?
hint: Who picks each one, and when can it change?

choices.text: A source identity is encrypted, and a session name is not
choices.why: Neither is secret; both are written into the log in plain text.

choices.text: It carries over to every chained role, and nobody can change it
choices.why: Right, and a trust policy can demand it. A session name is chosen afresh for every session.

choices.text: CloudTrail records source identities and drops session names
choices.why: The session name is in every log line, as the end of the session's ARN.

choices.text: moto checks a source identity, so the lab can prove it
choices.why: moto returned none at all; this part was not run.

prompt: For a caller to set a source identity, the role's trust policy must allow `sts:AssumeRole` and also `sts:___`.
hint: A verb, then the two words.

prompt: A session's key and a user's `AKIA` key leak on the same day. Why is the session's worth less to whoever found it?
hint: Look at `Expiration`.

choices.text: It stops working on its own after an hour
choices.why: Right. An `AKIA` key works until somebody notices and deletes it.

choices.text: It needs MFA to be used, and the `AKIA` key does not
choices.why: A session needs its token, not MFA; whoever holds all three values can use it.

choices.text: It only works from the machine that assumed the role
choices.why: Nothing ties it to a machine unless a condition does.

choices.text: AWS revokes every session when a leak is reported
choices.why: No such automatic revocation exists; the expiry is what limits it.

prompt: In moto, the session of `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` in `shop-prod` was refused a list of VPCs. In AWS, what would the same session be?
hint: What does AWS attach to the role it creates?

choices.text: The same: a role in a new account starts with no permissions
choices.why: That is moto's version. AWS attaches `AdministratorAccess` to this role.

choices.text: An administrator of `shop-prod`
choices.why: Right. AWS attaches `AdministratorAccess`, which is why who may assume the role matters so much.

choices.text: A read-only session, until the member account grants more
choices.why: No read-only policy is involved; it is full administration.

choices.text: The root user of `shop-prod`
choices.why: A role session is never the root user, even with every permission.

prompt: In the confused-deputy story, who is trying to misuse the shop's role?
hint: Not the one holding the permission.

choices.text: The monitoring company, which holds the permission
choices.why: The company is the deputy: it is used, not the user. It acts on whatever role ARN a customer gives it.

choices.text: Another of the company's customers, posing as the shop
choices.why: Right. They give the company the shop's role ARN as their own, and the external id is what stops the company acting on it.

choices.text: A developer of the shop with access to the role's ARN
choices.why: The shop's own people have their own ways in; the story is about a stranger using the company.

choices.text: The root user of the company's account
choices.why: Nothing in the story needs the company's root user; it works through the company's normal service.

prompt: What does the external id in the shop's trust policy establish?
hint: Not who the company is; the account already says that.

choices.text: That the request comes from the company's account
choices.why: The principal already establishes that, with the company's signature.

choices.text: A password that encrypts the session the company receives
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted with it; it is compared, as a string, with the trust policy.

choices.text: That the company is acting on the shop's own setup
choices.why: Right. The company sends the id of the customer who configured the request, so another customer cannot send the shop's.

choices.text: That the session will last no longer than one hour
choices.why: Duration is a separate setting; the external id says nothing about time.

prompt: Which of these did moto do differently from AWS in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them it judged as AWS does.

choices.text: Granted two hours on a role whose maximum was one
choices.why: Right. AWS refuses a duration above the role's maximum.

choices.text: Refused caio, whom the trust policy does not name
choices.why: That is exactly AWS's answer.

choices.text: Accepted an `AssumeRole` with no external id
choices.why: Right. AWS refuses it, since the `StringEquals` has nothing to match.

choices.text: Handed out a session in an account that does not exist
choices.why: Right. moto does not judge the other account's side at all.

choices.text: Refused bia a role her own policy does not name
choices.why: The caller's side is judged as AWS judges it.

choices.text: Refused a session of `deployer` a role that trusts `role/deployer`
choices.why: Right. AWS takes a role's ARN in a trust policy to mean its sessions.

prompt: Why does the lesson's profile use `credential_source = Environment` rather than `source_profile`?
hint: Where would a source profile's credentials live?

choices.text: `source_profile` cannot assume a role in another account
choices.why: It can; it is the usual form. The difference is where the signing credentials come from.

choices.text: No key has to be written to a file
choices.why: Right. A source profile with keys would mean writing admin's key into `~/.aws/credentials`.

choices.text: moto refuses profiles that name another profile
choices.why: moto never sees profiles; the command line resolves them before sending anything.

choices.text: `credential_source` makes the session last longer
choices.why: Duration is `duration_seconds`, a separate setting.

prompt: `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile shop-prod` answered with the account of `shop-prod`. What did the command line do first?
hint: Read the profile.

choices.text: It switched moto to the other account
choices.why: Nothing switches moto; the account follows the credentials that sign the call.

choices.text: It signed with admin's key and asked about shop-prod
choices.why: admin's key belongs to the management account and would have answered with it, as the last command did.

choices.text: It assumed the profile's role before anything
choices.why: Right. `configure list` showed `assume-role` as the type of the credentials.

choices.text: It read a key for shop-prod from `~/.aws/credentials`
choices.why: There is no such file in the lab, and no key for shop-prod anywhere.

prompt: The data team works in the management account and needs to read data in `shop-prod`. Which arrangement fits what this lesson taught?
hint: A door in the account being entered, and a key on the other side.

choices.text: IAM users for each of them in `shop-prod`, with access keys
choices.why: Long-term keys in a second account are exactly what a role avoids.

choices.text: A read role in `shop-prod` trusting the data team's role in management
choices.why: Right. The trust names one role, not the whole account, and that role's own policy allows `sts:AssumeRole` on it.

choices.text: Adding `shop-prod` to the `data` group
choices.why: A group holds users of one account; an account cannot join it.

choices.text: `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`, which every member account already has
choices.why: It works, and it is administration of the whole account, far more than reading.

prompt: A monitoring vendor says it needs no external id, because its AWS account number is unique. Why is that not enough?
hint: Whom does the account number identify?

choices.text: Account numbers can be reused once an account is closed
choices.why: The concern is not reuse; it is that one account serves every customer.

choices.text: Its account number is public, so anybody can sign as it
choices.why: Knowing an account number lets nobody sign as that account.

choices.text: It names the vendor, not which of the vendor's customers is asking
choices.why: Right. The same account assumes roles for every customer, and only the external id ties a request to one of them.

choices.text: Trust policies cannot name an account from outside the organisation
choices.why: They can, and third parties are named exactly that way.

prompt: In the lab, a cross-account `assume-role` succeeds. What has that proved?
hint: Which side of the agreement does moto judge across accounts?

choices.text: That the caller's own side allows the call, and nothing more
choices.why: Right. moto gave a session in an account that does not exist, so the trust policy over there was never read.

choices.text: That both trust and identity policies agree, as in AWS
choices.why: Only the identity side was judged. The trust side is the one moto skips across accounts.

choices.text: That the other account exists and holds the role
choices.why: `111122223333` exists nowhere, and moto answered all the same.

choices.text: That the role carries `AdministratorAccess`
choices.why: moto's `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` carries no policy at all.
